Weeping and Gnashing of Teeth
WEE-ping and NASH-ing of TEETH
n. phrase (eschatology; Synoptic judgment formula)
From Greek klauthmos (weeping, crying; from klaiō, to weep) + brugmos tōn odontōn (gnashing of the teeth; from brychō, to gnash, to grind the teeth). The Septuagint uses brugmos for teeth-gnashing in Job 16:9 and Psalm 35:16, signaling defiant rage rather than passive grief. Christ coined the eschatological formula and repeated it seven times in the Synoptic Gospels.

Biblical Definition

“Weeping and gnashing of teeth” is the phrase Christ uses in seven separate Synoptic contexts to describe the condition of those excluded from the kingdom of God at the final judgment. It appears in Matthew 8:12; 13:42; 13:50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30; and Luke 13:28 — spanning the parable of the dragnet, the parable of the wedding banquet, the parable of the faithful servant, and the parable of the talents. The repetition is deliberate: this is not a metaphorical flourish used once for effect but a fixed formula Christ returned to across varied parable contexts, each time describing the destination of those who appear religious but are ultimately excluded. The formula describes external exclusion (“outer darkness”) combined with internal anguish (“weeping and gnashing”). Weeping signals grief and recognition of what has been forfeited; gnashing of teeth signals rage, bitterness, and confirmed impenitence rather than the contrition that precedes repentance. This is not purgatorial purification but permanent confirmed rebellion. Luke 13:28 places the anguish in visible contrast to the blessedness of those inside: the condemned “see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God — but yourselves being cast out.” The sight of the blessedness they rejected intensifies the anguish they inherit. The formula is Christ's own vocabulary for eternal conscious punishment. The minister who suppresses it from preaching has silenced the One who coined it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Christ's seven-fold Synoptic formula for the condition of the finally condemned — cast into outer darkness, in grief over the kingdom forfeited and in confirmed unrepentant rage at their exclusion from the presence of God.

WEEPING AND GNASHING OF TEETH, n. phrase (eschatology). A fixed formula repeated seven times in the Synoptic Gospels to describe the irreversible condition of those excluded from the kingdom of God at the final judgment — grief for what is lost, confirmed rage at what is experienced.

The phrase is not a general description of suffering but a technical formula Christ repeated across parable contexts: the dragnet (Matt 13:50), the wedding banquet (Matt 22:13), the faithful servant (Matt 24:51), the talents (Matt 25:30), the prodigal region (Luke 13:28), and the centurion's household (Matt 8:12). The repetition argues for doctrinal weight, not merely rhetorical variety.

“Gnashing of teeth” in the Old Testament consistently signals defiance, rage, and hostility (Job 16:9; Ps 35:16; 37:12; Lam 2:16) — not sorrow leading to repentance but hardened enmity. The final state of the condemned is not bewildered grief but confirmed impenitence directed at God and His servants.

The paired location “outer darkness” (to skotos to exōteron) describes exclusion from the feast of the kingdom (Matt 8:11-12), which takes place in light and fellowship. The condemned are not absent from consciousness; they are present enough to recognize what they have lost and in whose presence they stand excluded.

Annihilationism, which teaches that the wicked are extinguished rather than eternally punished, cannot accommodate the ongoing present-tense formula: “there shall be weeping and gnashing” implies a continuing condition, not a terminal event. The Reformed confession of eternal conscious punishment is the natural reading of the formula Christ Himself repeatedly used.

Key Scripture

Matthew 8:12 — "But the sons of the kingdom shall be cast out into the outer darkness. In that place there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.""

Matthew 13:42 — "And will cast them into the furnace of fire — in that place there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth."

Luke 13:28 — "There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God — but yourselves being cast out."

Matthew 25:30 — "And cast out the worthless slave into the outer darkness. In that place there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth."

Modern Corruption

Annihilationism denies the ongoing conscious dimension of the formula; universalism treats the gnashing as temporary purgation; sentimental evangelicalism suppresses the formula from preaching as unloving, silencing Christ's own words.

expand to see more

Annihilationism (Clark Pinnock, Edward Fudge, and John Stott in his later writings) argues that the wicked are ultimately extinguished rather than consciously punished forever. This reading cannot satisfy the formula: the present-tense phrase “there shall be weeping and gnashing” implies a continuing condition, not a terminal state. Annihilationists typically argue that aiōnios (eternal) modifies the consequences of punishment rather than its duration. But the formula describes an experience (“weeping,” “gnashing”), not a consequence, and experience requires a conscious subject to continue experiencing it. The Old Testament background of “gnashing” (rage, defiance) confirms that the condemned are not being extinguished but confirmed in their hostility.

Sentimental evangelicalism — the therapeutic gospel that centers God's love while suppressing His justice — cannot preach this formula. Rob Bell's Love Wins (2011) represents the cultural pressure to dissolve the formula's severity into hopeful uncertainty. If eternal conscious punishment is the destination of the unrepentant, then every sermon without the summons to flee is not pastoral sensitivity but pastoral negligence. Christ's seven uses of the formula answer the objection that the warning is unloving: He repeated it precisely because the urgency of the warning required repetition across every kind of audience. The minister who cannot preach “weeping and gnashing of teeth” because it might offend has forgotten who coined the phrase and for whose sake He coined it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Greek klauthmos (weeping) and brugmos tōn odontōn (gnashing of teeth); the Old Testament Septuagint background of brugmos marks defiant rage, not passive suffering, identifying the condemned's posture as confirmed impenitence.

expand to see more

Greek klauthmos (κλαυθμός) — weeping, crying; from klaiō (to weep); in the New Testament, weeping associated with grief at loss (John 11:33; Rev 18:15); in the eschatological formula, the grief is for the forfeited kingdom and the recognition of irreversible exclusion.

Greek brugmos (βρυγμός) — gnashing; from brychō (to gnash, to grind the teeth); in classical and Septuagint usage, teeth-gnashing marks rage, defiance, and hostility (Acts 7:54, the crowd gnashing at Stephen before his martyrdom).

Greek tōn odontōn (τῶν ὀδόντων) — of the teeth; the genitive of odous (tooth); the combination brugmos tōn odontōn is a set phrase in the Septuagint (Job 16:9; Ps 35:16) for hostile fury directed against God's servants.

Greek to skotos to exōteron (τὸ σκότος τὸ ἐξώτερον) — the outer darkness; found three times in Matthew (8:12; 22:13; 25:30); the “outer” dimension contrasts with the inner light of the feast, underscoring that damnation is exclusion from the presence and fellowship of God.

Hebrew ḥārak shinnayim — gnashing of teeth (Lam 2:16; Ps 35:16); the Old Testament background makes clear that gnashing signals defiant hostility, not passive suffering, confirming the formula describes the impenitent rage of the confirmed rebel against God.

Usage

"Faithful preaching of this formula is an act of love: the congregation that never hears “weeping and gnashing of teeth” from the pulpit has not been sheltered from a hard doctrine but robbed of the urgency that belongs to every genuine gospel call."

"The formula refutes purgatorial thinking: there is no penitent weeping in a refining state leading to eventual release — the weeping of the formula is accompanied by confirmed gnashing, marking the condemned as impenitent, not merely unrefined."

"For the believer, this formula is not a cause of terror but of worship: we who deserved the outer darkness are seated at the feast — not by our merit but by the blood of the One who bore the outer darkness for us, and the seriousness of what we escaped must continually drive us to gratitude."
